newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Germany's Kinkel pledges support for Bulgaria.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Kinkel pledges support for Bulgaria.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel visited Bulgaria on Thursday with a pledge of support for the new government and its efforts to revive the economy.
On a three-hour visit to Bulgaria's second city of Plovdiv, Kinkel assured his hosts of Germany's backing for their applications to join NATO and the European Union.

"Bulgaria belongs to Europe. Bulgaria is welcome in the European Union as soon as possible," Kinkel said after talks with President Petar Stoyanov at a 19th century merchant's house in Plovdiv's old town.

Kinkel pledged German support at next month's donor meeting in Brussels of the G-24 industrialised countries, which will draw up a financing package to accompany an International Monetary Fund standby accord agreed in principle last week. He declined to give a figure.

Corruption and the failure of successive governments to implement reforms brought the economy to the brink of collapse. The IMF prescribed a tough fixed exchange rate regime as a last resort after previous programmes failed.
Kinkel warned that measures to rescue the economy were painful but inevitable. "You will make it, it will be tough but the bitter medicine will ensure that you recover," he said.

Bulgaria has little hope of entering the EU or NATO in the first wave of eastern expansion, but both groups see it as a force for stability in the Balkans, and with an eye on Albania and Serbia are keen to keep it in their sphere of influence.
Kinkel said that countries which failed to make it into the first wave should not feel abandoned.
"The door will stay open and we will find ways to give the feeling to those who don't make it that they are welcome and the way of course stays open," he told reporters.
Bulgaria has attracted a string of prominent visitors since a 30-day protest campaign fuelled by economic hardship toppled the Socialist government last month.

Bulgaria has an association accord with the EU, and one of the first decisions of the new interim cabinet was to make a clear statement of their desire to join NATO, an issue on which the Socialists had always been ambivalent for fear of upsetting their traditional allies in Moscow.
Kinkel signed a technical cooperation accord with Bulgaria, and delivered a private donation of medical supplies worth 40,000 marks to the regional hospital in Pazardzhik.

He arrived in Bulgaria from Turkey, where he assured the Ankara government that it had a place in Europe, but listed human rights problems, economic troubles, an armed Kurdish rebellion and quarrels with EU member Greece as serious obstacles to eventual Turkish membership in the EU.
